sentences.text: Companies buy because billing has to track usage: "we pay for what we bill, so it has to follow our usage".
Finance teams also want revenue recognized "the day usage posts".
The main objection is that buyers are "worried about invoice surprises for our customers".
The most common signer is the Finance leader, and we win 38% of 212 opportunities at a median deal size of $41k over a 78 days cycle.
Fintech buyers in this segment want an "audit trail for every charge" because regulators ask for it.
The main objection is capacity: the finance team is "only two people" and worries about the workload.
The CFO is the one raising concerns, so expect finance to lead the decision and sign.
Buyers also look at other vendors, and we win 29% of 96 opportunities, with a $36k median deal and a 64 days cycle on won deals.
Developer tools companies buy because their "engineers want an api first billing layer".
The main objection is build versus buy, with buyers saying "we can build this ourselves in a quarter", and security review can also slow deals, sometimes taking "longer than the eval".
Across 143 opportunities the win rate is 22% with a median deal size of $29k, and the most common signer is the Head of engineering.
In healthcare software, compliance comes first: the security lead "needs HIPAA terms before any call" and legal asked for a BAA we could not give.
Procurement is slow, and won deals took 131 days to close.
The segment has a 9% win rate across 77 opportunities, with a median deal size of $52k, and these notes record objections rather than reasons for winning.
The notes do not say why buyers choose us or who signs, only that security, legal and procurement each act as gatekeepers.
Marketplaces win 17% of 58 opportunities, and the main objection is that the product misses their real pain: "our payouts are the hard part, not invoices".
Buyers also see their core revenue as outside billing, saying "take rate revenue is not billing" and that the product "does not touch our seller fees".
A finance vice president voiced the take rate objection, so finance leadership weighs in, though the quotes do not confirm who signs.
The quotes give no reason why marketplaces buy, and the median deal size is $33k.
DACH wins 12% of 44 opportunities, and won deals take 102 days to close.
The notes record objections only, not reasons to buy, and they center on being local: a German entity "needs local invoicing rules" and a controller "only works with local vendors".
Who signs is unknown, since buyers say "org charts are private here" and no common signer shows up in the data.
Across 310 opportunities, with a 27% win rate and a $44k median deal, buyers in this segment already run their business in the CRM and want quotes to "flow to billing" without extra steps.
A competing billing tool enters these deals because of its connector to that CRM, so expect to be judged on how well your own integration holds up.
Companies in this segment buy to consolidate, with the CFO saying they want "one system for all business units".
The main objections are process ones: buyers say "we need a six month legal review" and "five stakeholders have to approve".
That friction shows in the results, with an 8% win rate across 121 opportunities and won deals taking 156 days at a median deal size of $88k.
The CFO is the likely signer, but plan for a group of approvers rather than a single yes.
Brazil has 9 opportunities with a 56% win rate, and the reason to buy we have is that marketplaces there "bill in reais and need local tax".
The notes for this segment say nothing about objections or who signs, so local billing and tax support is the only buying driver on record.
In the seat pricing segment, the main objection we hear is that seat based pricing is "a poor fit for usage billing", which leads buyers to keep their current tool.
Across 180 opportunities in this segment, the win rate is 14%, consistent with that pricing objection.
Data infrastructure companies buy because usage metering is hard to get right, and they bill by volume and need it exact.
The main objection comes from the controller, who doubts revenue recognition for prepaid commits.
The controller is the finance voice to win over, though the quotes do not say who signs.
Across 88 opportunities the win rate is 33%, with a median deal size of $47k and won deals closing in 71 days.
Logistics software buyers want billing to keep pace with operations, since the VP of operations "wants invoices to follow shipments".
The main objection is that "per shipment pricing makes forecasting hard", so expect pushback on how usage-based charges are budgeted.
Deals often mean displacing an incumbent billing vendor, and the VP of operations is the senior buyer we see driving the decision.
Across 64 opportunities we win 19%, at a median deal size of $31k.
Education buyers choose us for term based billing, though the segment is hard to win, with an 11% win rate across 39 opportunities.
The main objection is timing, since "budgets are set once a year", so deals need to line up with the annual planning cycle.
The most common signer is the Finance leader, who owns that annual budget and should be engaged early.
Media buyers like that ad impressions can be billed directly, and the controller is the one who raised it.
The main objection is that ad credits are "messy to recognize".
Some buyers ask about a competing product, so expect comparisons.
Across 47 opportunities the win rate is 21%, and won deals take 59 days to close.
E-commerce buyers come to us because "subscription boxes need proration done right", across 102 opportunities with a $24k median deal size and a 16% win rate.
The main objections are that they already use a billing add on, or that checkout is handled by the shop platform.
The checkout objection came from a CFO, so finance is the voice to win over, though the quotes do not show who signs.
Across 31 government opportunities the win rate is 6%, and won deals take 190 days, which matches the procurement hurdles buyers raise.
An elected official can hold up a deal by asking for a "public tender first".
The controller signs but "cannot sign without a framework contract", so confirm early whether one exists or must be set up.
These notes only show objections, not reasons to buy, so learn the buying motive on discovery calls.
Fintech buyers pick us because "usage based fees map to how our banks bill us".
Across 301 opportunities the segment wins 25% of the time, with a median deal size of $39k.
A controller was involved on the buying side and compared us against a competitor, so expect finance to sign.
No usable objection was recorded for this segment.
IT services companies buy because resellers "need billing that sums usage across clients".
This segment shows a 13% win rate across 66 opportunities, so that billing need alone is not closing most deals.
The only objection on file is not a real customer objection, and no quote says who signs.
Companies with mixed pricing buy because they sell seats plus usage and want "both on one invoice" and "one source of revenue truth".
A rival tool they tried "handled seats but not overage", which leaves the gap we fill.
The main objection is "migration risk during quarter close", so plan the cutover around their close.
The most common signer is the Finance leader, and the segment shows a 24% win rate across 155 opportunities, a $37k median deal and an 83 days won-deal cycle.
In this segment of small companies, the reason to buy is forward looking: they expect usage billing to matter once they launch tiers.
The common objection is that "a spreadsheet works for us for now", which helps explain a 10% win rate across 240 opportunities.
The founder signs everything and wants a cheap tool, so expect price pressure around a median deal size of $12k.
Add a rule to the ideal customer profile that the pricing model equals Usage.
Across 212 opportunities, deals with Usage pricing won 38% of the time (range 32% to 45%), clearly higher than the 16% win rate for the rest.
Add a rule that gives 15 points to accounts whose pricing model is Usage.
Across 212 opportunities, Usage pricing deals won 38% of the time (range 32% to 45%) against 16% for the rest, a clearly higher result.
Add a rule to the ideal customer profile that gives accounts in the Fintech industry a weight of 10.
Across 140 Fintech opportunities the win rate was 32% (range 25% to 40%), clearly higher than the 18% win rate for the rest of the deals.
Add a rule to the ideal customer profile that scores accounts higher when Signer role findable is Yes.
Across 300 opportunities where Signer role findable was Yes, deals were won 29% of the time (range 24% to 34%), compared with 14% for the rest, which is clearly higher.
Add a rule that gives weight 5 to accounts whose Technology includes NetSuite.
Across 95 opportunities, deals with NetSuite won 32% of the time (range 23% to 41%) compared with 19% for the rest, a clearly higher win rate, and timing was the most common loss reason.
Add a rule to the ideal customer profile that gives weight to accounts in the 120 to 499 size band.
Across 400 opportunities in that band, deals were won at 30% (range 26% to 35%), compared with 15% for all other deals, a clearly higher win rate.
Remove the rule that favors accounts whose Technology includes Salesforce.
Across 310 opportunities, deals with Salesforce won 27% (range 22% to 32%) against 22% for the rest, and that gap was explained by company size rather than the technology itself.
Remove the rule that favors accounts whose Technology includes HubSpot.
Across 180 opportunities, HubSpot accounts won 24% (range 19% to 31%) against 23% for the rest, and the deals showed that gap was explained by size, not by HubSpot.
Remove the rule that favors accounts with an HQ city of Austin from the ideal customer profile.
Across 70 opportunities, Austin deals won 17% of the time (range 10% to 28%) against 16% for the rest, so the deals showed no clear difference.
Remove the rule that targets companies with a founding year after 2015.
Across 260 opportunities, companies founded after 2015 won 21% of deals against 20% for the rest, and the deals showed that difference is explained by company size rather than founding year.
Give the Usage pricing model a weight of 20 in the ideal customer profile.
Across 212 opportunities, deals with Usage pricing won 38% of the time (range 32% to 45%), compared with 16% for the rest, which is clearly higher.
Give accounts in the 120 to 1,999 size band more weight in the ideal customer profile.
Across 520 opportunities in this size band, deals were won at 29% (range 25% to 33%), clearly higher than the 14% win rate for all other accounts.
Change the weight on Industry equals Developer tools to 4 in the ideal customer profile.
Across 143 opportunities, Developer tools deals won at 22% (range 16% to 30%), the same as the 22% for all other deals, so the deals showed no clear difference.
Add Healthcare software as an excluded industry in the ideal customer profile.
Across 77 Healthcare software opportunities the win rate was 9% (range 4% to 18%), clearly lower than 23% for the rest, and compliance was the top loss reason.
Add Government to the Industry exclusions in the ideal customer profile.
Across 31 Government opportunities the win rate was 6% (range 2% to 21%), clearly lower than the 21% for all other deals, and timing was the most common loss reason.
Add an exclusion to the ideal customer profile for accounts where Country equals Brazil.
The 9 Brazil opportunities won at 56%, with a range of 27% to 81%, against 17% for all other deals, so the deals did not give a clear signal.
Accounts in the 2,000 to 4,999 size band will now score lower in the ideal customer profile.
Across 121 opportunities in this size band, deals won 8% of the time (range 5% to 15%) compared with 17% for the rest, and the most common loss reason was no decision.
Lower the score for Healthcare software accounts in the Industry field by 8 points.
Across 77 Healthcare software opportunities the win rate was 9% (range 4% to 18%) against 23% for the rest, clearly lower, and the most common loss reason was compliance.
Deals in the DACH region will now take a penalty in the ideal customer profile score.
Across 44 DACH opportunities the win rate was 11% (range 5% to 24%), compared with 20% for all other regions, which is clearly lower.
Add a rule to the profile that gives extra weight to opportunities where the Country is United States.
The 650 United States opportunities won at 23% (range 20% to 26%) compared with 24% for the rest, so the deals did not show a clear difference.
